title: Assemble a mini chopper so it is ready to run, then pulse it once
instruction: Assemble the mini chopper so it is ready to run, then pulse it once. Touch the blade only by its hub. Finish with both arms back where they started.
context: A mini chopper is one of the most common small kitchen appliances, and it is put together before every use: the blade goes on its pin, and the motor runs only once its top is twisted fully home, which closes its safety switch. The light bowl turns with the motor top unless it is held, so it takes two hands, the kind of everyday job a home-assistance robot would do for someone with weak or painful hands.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. All parts are at real size and mass. (1) The bowl of a cordless electric mini chopper, loose on the table, its middle 25.5 cm forward and 5 cm right of the centre line: clear SAN plastic, 0.14 kg, 9.0 cm across inside and 9.7 cm outside, its rim 7.4 cm above its underside (about 400 ml), standing on a black rubber foot ring; its floor is 0.9 cm up, and a stainless pin 8 mm across rises from the middle to 4.9 cm (a 5 mm tip to 5.3 cm). On its left side a handle: a round upright bar 2.0 cm across, its axis 9.2 cm from the bowl's axis, from 1.6 to 6.8 cm up, joined to the wall by two arms 1.4 cm wide, 1.6-2.4 cm and 5.2-6.0 cm up (below the motor top's collar, which reaches down to 6.4 cm when seated). Just under the rim, on the side away from the arms, a dark dot (the open mark), and 30 degrees anticlockwise from it (seen from above) a dark bar (the lock mark). (2) The S-blade, loose: two stainless blades 1.4 cm wide and 2 mm thick, reaching 4.0 cm from the axis, 6 and 15 mm up a grey plastic hub 2.3 cm across and 4.2 cm tall that is open at the top (the drive socket); 35 g. It stands on its storage post, fixed, 33.5 cm forward and 17.5 cm right: a beech disc 6 cm across and 8 mm thick with an 8 mm peg 4 cm tall. (3) The motor top, loose, standing on the table 19.5 cm forward and 17 cm right: white ABS, 0.28 kg in all (motor and battery); a plate 10.5 cm across with a collar 1 cm deep underneath that fits round the bowl's rim (9.9 cm inside), a housing 6.8 cm across whose top is 5.6 cm above the plate's underside, a light on top (dark), a dark arrow on the plate's edge pointing away from the arms, and on its right side a twist grip: a fin 1.2 cm thick, 2.5 cm tall, reaching 7.6 cm from its axis. In the middle of the housing's top is the PULSE button, a real sprung push button: a grey ABS cap 3.4 cm across (10 g) standing 4 mm proud on a slide with 3.5 mm of travel, its preloaded spring pushing up with 4 N at rest, 6 N at its switch point 2 mm down and 7.5 N at its stop. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: The motor top is caught by the bowl's bayonet once it is set down on the rim (its plate's underside at most 0.6 mm above the rim) with its middle within 8 mm of the bowl's axis, tilted at most 8 degrees against the bowl and its arrow within 14 degrees of the open mark. It then stays where it was left until it is turned with 0.3 N m. Turned 28.5 degrees anticlockwise from the open mark it clicks: a detent holds it against its stop at 31.5 degrees until it is forced back below 28.5 degrees (0.48 N m). Turned back to within 8 degrees of the open mark and pulled up (its plate more than 0.8 mm above the rim for 3 control steps), it comes off. Locked is checked live, never latched: the motor top caught, seated (its middle within 3 mm of the bowl's axis, its plate within 2.5 mm of the rim, tilted at most 3 degrees) and turned at least 28.5 degrees. The light is on while it is locked. PULSE's switch closes when the button is pushed 2 mm down its slide and opens again when it is back above 1 mm; the motor runs while the switch is closed and the motor top is locked, and the blade, if on its pin, then spins at 25 rad/s. A pulse is the motor starting with the blade on its pin. A hand over or resting on the button without pushing it 2 mm down does nothing. The blade is on its pin when its hub's axis is within 4 mm of the pin's, the hub's bottom within 4 mm of the bowl's floor, and it is tilted at most 10 degrees. The score is 0.0 once a fingertip (a gripper's fingertip centre or its pads' tips) has come within 1.5 cm of the middle line of either blade's cutting part (the 1.4 cm wide blade beyond 2 cm from the hub's axis), that is, within about 8 mm of its edges. Otherwise 1.0: exactly one pulse, and at the end PULSE let go (its switch open), the motor top still locked, the blade on its pin, the bowl standing on the table (tilted less than 5 degrees, raised less than 4 mm) and both arms back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre within 5 cm of its start); 0.75: at least one pulse; 0.5: the motor top locked and the blade on its pin at the end; 0.25: the blade on its pin at the end; else 0.0. In a real trial, use a mini chopper whose top button needs about 6 N to switch (typical units take 5-15 N): a pulse is the motor starting, heard and seen as the blade turning, with the top's arrow at its lock mark and its light on, and the end state is checked the same way after the arms are home. Judged at the end of the trial, which ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the bowl, the motor top, its button and the blade still.
reset_notes: Stand the blade back on its storage post, the motor top back on the table where it started (arrow pointing forward), and the empty bowl back in its place with its handle to the left.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz); real-size, real-mass parts. PULSE is a real sprung slide (3.5 mm travel, 6 N at its switch point). Simplified: the bayonet is a joint (catch, 0.3 N m friction spring, detent, stop, release at the open mark), not lug contacts; the switches are rules on the button's travel and the top's live pose; the motor isn't modelled: while it runs the blade's speed is set (nothing is chopped); the clear wall is drawn only at rim, foot and seams.
